deep_dive.headline: The AI spend question has no owner: token cost sits between finance, engineering, security and procurement, and FinOps practitioners now rank it their top challenge
deep_dive.source_name: FinOps Foundation, 'Tokenomics: Managing AI Value in SaaS Model Token Costs'
deep_dive.summary: The FinOps Foundation's practitioner guide, last updated 3 June 2026, reports that its practitioner survey identified managing the cost and use of tokens in SaaS-model AI as the top challenge facing practitioners today. The guide is a framework for token cost governance rather than a survey report — verified on fetch, it carries no organisation counts or budget-overrun percentages. Separately reported in the same sweep but NOT in this document: a State of FinOps 2026 survey of 1,192 organisations managing $83bn of annual cloud and technology spend, with 98% now tracking AI spending against 31% in 2024, and 73% reporting AI spend exceeded their annual budget. Industry practice reporting describes the emerging pattern as a small team between finance and engineering reporting to the CTO or VP Engineering owning visibility, governance and vendor negotiation, typically landing with a platform or AI-enablement lead who owns the gateway, the routing policy and the dashboards, with job titles including AI Cost Engineer, LLM FinOps Lead and ML Platform Cost Owner.
deep_dive.so_what: Budget ownership is the operating-model decision leaders are least prepared for: the spend is variable, generated by engineering choices, and currently belongs to nobody in particular.
deep_dive.chartable_data: 98% tracking against 31% in 2024 with 73% over budget is a strong three-stat panel IF verified; the four-way ownership split (finance / engineering / security / procurement) is a diagram.
deep_dive.notes: SPLIT SOURCING — the finops.org page WAS fetched and verified, and it does NOT contain the 1,192 / $83bn / 98% / 73% figures. Those come from secondary write-ups of a separate 'State of FinOps 2026' report. Phase 3 MUST locate and fetch that report before any of those four numbers is printed; if it cannot be found, print only the fetched 'top challenge' finding. Emerging-role titles are practitioner-blog sourced and should be framed as reported practice, not data.

deep_dive.headline: Agent identity becomes the enforcement point: two-thirds of organisations apply weaker controls to agents than to humans, and only 34% apply human-grade controls
deep_dive.source_name: Okta, 'AI Agents at Work 2026: Securing the agentic enterprise'
deep_dive.summary: Okta's position is that every AI agent should be a first-class identity with its own lifecycle and granular permissions, and its research reports that only 34% of organisations apply human-grade security controls to agents, with nearly two-thirds applying weaker controls to agents than to employees. Agent SSO registers an agent as a first-class identity in Okta's Universal Directory and issues short-lived governed tokens instead of the static API keys agents normally carry. Shadow agents created by individual employees are described across 2026 surveys as the largest blind spot. On standards, the MCP November 2025 specification revision added Cross App Access semantics and explicit OAuth 2.1 authorisation-server requirements, with Anthropic's reference implementation requiring PKCE and dynamic client registration. Microsoft-centric organisations reach coverage fastest through Entra Agent ID; multi-vendor estates running agents across five or more platforms benefit most from a fabric approach.
deep_dive.so_what: Identity is where 'which agent may do what' stops being a policy document and becomes an enforceable control — and it is the limb of the operating model most likely to already have an owner in a bank.
deep_dive.chartable_data: 34% applying human-grade controls against ~66% applying weaker ones is a single strong two-segment figure; static API key versus short-lived governed token is a two-column comparison.
deep_dive.notes: DATE UNPINNED — published_date 2026-01-01 is a PLACEHOLDER; Phase 3 must pin the Okta report's date. VENDOR RESEARCH from an identity vendor describing an identity problem — attribute and flag the interest. The two-thirds and 34% figures should be read as two framings of the same Okta finding, not two independent data points.

deep_dive.headline: UK prudential expectations already cover this: SS1/23 model risk management, senior-manager accountability, and audit trails sufficient to investigate AI-caused customer harm
deep_dive.source_name: Prudential Regulation Authority SS1/23 and FCA / Bank of England AI expectations (via practitioner analysis)
deep_dive.summary: SS1/23, the PRA's first supervisory statement dedicated to model risk management, applies to UK-incorporated banks, building societies and PRA-designated investment firms with internal model approval for regulatory capital, and emphasises board-level accountability and integration into the wider risk framework. UK financial services AI is governed across three regulators — the FCA for conduct, the PRA for prudential soundness and the Bank of England for financial stability — applying existing rules including the senior managers regime, operational resilience and Consumer Duty. Practitioner analysis of 2026 expectations describes an AI inventory covering purpose and scope, data used, decisions influenced, affected populations and risk classification; where AI system failures cause customer harm, firms must hold audit trails sufficient to investigate and report accurately to the FCA, and the PRA expects firms to be inspection-ready with documented evidence of model decisions, changes and validation outcomes. The Bank of England and FCA's third AI survey found 75% of firms already using AI, 55% of use cases carrying some automated decision-making, 46% of firms reporting only partial understanding of the AI they use against 34% claiming complete understanding, and 84% having an accountable person for their AI framework.
deep_dive.so_what: It is the answer to why a bank customer will ask a supplier for evidence rather than assurance — the accountability and audit-trail expectations already exist and are being read onto AI without new rules.
deep_dive.chartable_data: Four survey figures (75% using AI / 55% with automated decisioning / 46% partial understanding vs 34% complete / 84% with an accountable person) make a clean bar set.
deep_dive.notes: DATES MIXED AND UNPINNED — SS1/23 was issued in 2023; the BoE/FCA third AI survey reported here was published November 2024; the 2026 practitioner analyses are undated secondary sources. published_date 2026-01-01 is a PLACEHOLDER. Phase 3 must source the survey figures from the Bank of England / FCA primaries before print and date them as 2024. AUDIENCE GATE: per the spec, bank-regulator material is At a Glance / On the Radar / Other News in a weekly and is background framing in a deep dive — never the spine.

deep_dive.headline: The EU's high-risk deadline moved, but the record-keeping and human-oversight obligations did not
deep_dive.source_name: EU AI Act timeline and the Digital Omnibus on AI (via Covington Inside Global Tech / Holland & Knight)
deep_dive.summary: 2 August 2026 had been the binding application date for high-risk obligations under Articles 9-17 (providers) and Article 26 (deployers). On 7 May 2026 Council, Parliament and Commission negotiators reached a provisional agreement on a Digital Omnibus on AI mixing timeline extensions, simplification and a small number of substantive changes; Annex III high-risk obligations were postponed from 2 August 2026 to 2 December 2027. The AI Act's core requirements remain governance, transparency, record-keeping, human oversight, robustness, cybersecurity and lifecycle management, with penalties up to EUR 15m or 3% of global annual turnover. DORA, separately, does not regulate AI but places ICT risk-management obligations on financial entities, which practitioner analysis reads as covering an agent that accesses data, takes actions and talks to other systems as an ICT system in its own right.
deep_dive.so_what: The deadline moved; the shape of the evidence did not — record-keeping, human oversight and lifecycle management are the same artefacts an internal agent platform has to produce anyway.
deep_dive.chartable_data: A dated timeline (2 Aug 2026 original / 7 May 2026 provisional agreement / 2 Dec 2027 Annex III) is the natural treatment.
deep_dive.notes: OUT OF WINDOW (7 May 2026 agreement; 28 May 2026 analysis) — state dates. Regulatory detail here is from law-firm commentary, not the Official Journal; Phase 3 must confirm the postponement's legal status before stating it as settled — a provisional agreement is not adopted law. The DORA-covers-agents reading is practitioner interpretation, not a regulator statement, and must be framed as such. AUDIENCE GATE: background only.

deep_dive.headline: Gartner's platform-engineering read: governance models built for human developers are showing cracks, and 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by end-2027
deep_dive.source_name: Gartner Hype Cycle for Platform Engineering 2026 and Gartner agentic-AI predictions (via secondary analysis)
deep_dive.summary: Secondary analysis of the Gartner Hype Cycle for Platform Engineering 2026 reports its framing that platform-engineering decisions over the next twelve months determine whether organisations can scale AI responsibly, that agents are entering software delivery as autonomous participants, that agentic workloads generate new cost structures, and that governance models built for human developers are showing cracks. Gartner separately predicts more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by end-2027, driven by escalating costs, unclear business value and inadequate risk controls, and forecasts the worldwide AI platforms and models market growing 63% in 2026. A widely-cited earlier Gartner projection holds that 80% of software organisations will have platform teams by 2026.
deep_dive.so_what: The cancellation prediction is the counterpoint the deep dive needs: the operating-model redesign is not a formality, and the named causes are cost, value and controls rather than capability.
deep_dive.chartable_data: 40% cancellation by 2027, 63% market growth in 2026 and 80% of orgs with platform teams are three stat tiles but from three different Gartner outputs — label each separately, do not combine.
deep_dive.notes: MOSTLY SECONDARY-SOURCED — only the 20 July 2026 market-forecast press release is a Gartner primary and is behind the URL given; the Hype Cycle framing and the 40% cancellation prediction reach this run through vendor blogs (TrueFoundry, digitalapplied, Itential). Phase 3 must find Gartner primaries for the 40% figure or attribute it as 'reported'. The 80% platform-teams figure dates from an older prediction and must not be presented as new.

deep_dive.headline: Pragmatic Engineer's 900-plus-respondent survey finds the engineer/manager division dissolving, with nothing arriving to replace it
deep_dive.source_name: The Pragmatic Engineer (Gergely Orosz), 'The impact of AI on software engineers in 2026'
deep_dive.summary: A survey of more than 900 engineers and engineering leaders. Engineers orchestrate and context-switch more; engineering managers can be more hands-on; the two roles are converging. The reported framing is that the division of responsibilities between engineer and EM was doing structural work few leaders ever named, and coding agents are dissolving it without a replacement. A related finding: code production is accelerating faster than organisational ownership, creating ambiguity about accountability when production incidents involve AI-generated code.
deep_dive.so_what: Role convergence is a design problem, not a culture problem — and accountability for AI-generated code in production is the decision right most organisations have not assigned.
deep_dive.chartable_data: No hard percentages captured this run beyond the 900+ sample; treat as qualitative unless Phase 3 recovers figures.

deep_dive.headline: CNCF frames the agent as a platform persona: RBAC, quotas and policy applied to agents the way they are applied to people
deep_dive.source_name: CNCF, 'Platform engineering for the agentic enterprise: managing applications, resources, and AI agents'
deep_dive.summary: The piece argues that a platform team's job has always been to balance enablement against control, and that with agents both sides sharpen. Mature platforms in 2026 treat agents as another user persona with RBAC permissions, resource quotas and governance policies. Related practitioner guidance in the same sweep holds that every agent should have a unique identity, an accountable human owner and an expiration date, with least privilege applied to individual actions, environments, resources and time windows rather than at account level.
deep_dive.so_what: It converts 'who owns the agents' into an answer a platform lead already knows how to give — the same controls, applied to a new persona.
deep_dive.chartable_data: Agent-as-persona control set (identity / accountable owner / expiry / RBAC / quota / policy) is a six-cell control table.
deep_dive.notes: OUT OF WINDOW (21 July 2026) — state the date. Not fetched this run; claims are search-summary-sourced and Phase 3 should verify before quoting. Foundation blog, vendor-neutral, but individual authorship not captured.
